nodes.label: Jamaica’s mills

nodes.label: Louisiana

nodes.label: Slave trade volume

nodes.label: Raffald

nodes.label: Qing coast
nodes.full: The Qing evacuate the coast and take Taiwan in 1683.

nodes.label: Refineries
nodes.full: Amsterdam’s refineries go from 40 to 110, London’s reach 80.

nodes.full: The sugar islands lose their forests, 1650–1750.

nodes.label: Islands’ worth
nodes.full: The sugar islands’ exports are worth £4.5 million to Britain and £8.25 million to France in 1789.

edges: Walvin: sugar took hold in Barbados by 1640 with Brazilian experience, and the island exported 7,000 tons by 1650.
Buttery ties Barbados’s turn to sugar to the replacement of indentured Europeans by enslaved Africans, ten in 1627 to thousands by the 1640s.
Buttery: the Act for the Governing of Negroes of 1661 followed as the enslaved population on Barbados grew.
Buttery sets the seven recorded mutinies of 1640–1713 beside the law’s harsh punishments and the secrecy needed for a rising.
Fox’s visit to Barbados in 1671 and the planters’ hostility to teaching slaves came ten years after the 1661 Act.
Ligon’s history (1647–50) and Fox’s visit (1671) are the two principal English accounts, in Buttery, of Barbados’s early plantation society.
Walvin: by c.1700 Barbados’s distilleries had copper stills, and rum exports passed half a million gallons a year by the 1690s.
Walvin: the illness blamed on rum was traced in 1745 to lead piping in the local distilleries.
Walvin: Barbados’s rum went to Africa from 1680 and found a market on the Gold Coast by c.1700.
Barbados sent its rum chiefly to New England, where Massachusetts distilleries made 2.7 million gallons by the mid-century.
Walvin: British taxes on molasses and sugar roused New England against Britain as its distillers used cheap smuggled French molasses.
Walvin ties the resentment of the Molasses and Sugar Acts to the break of 1776 and the trade’s adjustment during the war.
Walvin names the Navigation Acts and the later duties on sugar and molasses together as the British restrictions that alienated America.
Jamaica, taken in 1655, overtook Barbados by 1712, with 57 mills in 1670 and 1,061 in 1786.
Walvin’s totals for the Caribbean’s rise include Jamaica’s 36,000 tons of the 1770 total of over 200,000.
Saint-Domingue’s 60,000 tons of 1770 was the largest single share of the Caribbean’s output.
Smith: the Treaty of Ryswick of 1697 divided Hispaniola, and the French colony then became the most productive sugar island.
Smith and Walvin together: Saint-Domingue’s 790,000 imported Africans, and 500,000 enslaved to 32,000 whites in 1789.
Smith: the white minority’s rule over 500,000 enslaved people gave way to the revolt of 1791 that ended in Haitian independence.
Walvin: Louisiana sugar flourished from the 1790s in the wake of the Haitian revolution.
Walvin: the collapse of Saint-Domingue is the push for France to find sugar elsewhere, and beet.
Achard, Marggraf’s student, perfected the beet process and presented its sugar to the king of Prussia in 1799.
Walvin: the leap of Caribbean sugar output ‘could not have happened’ without the transport of millions of Africans.
Buttery’s account of the Zong of 1781 is one of the horror stories of the Atlantic crossing that Walvin counts in the trade’s volume.
Walvin: the legal cases of the 1770s included whether traders could claim insurance for Africans thrown overboard, the question the Zong case raised.
Buttery: horror stories like the Zong drove the sugar boycott and the Quaker case against slave-grown sugar.
Buttery presents the Wedgwood medallion and William Fox’s calculation among the abolitionist campaign’s symbols.
Walvin: smuggling thrived until the tea duties were slashed in 1784.
Tea, sugar and coffee are Mintz’s ‘groceries’, whose share of British imports doubled in the century.
Mintz sets Hanway’s attack on the poor’s tea and sugar against the refiners who pressed for wider markets.
Mintz follows Hanway’s complaint with Eden’s budgets of 1797 showing labouring families’ sugar and tea.
Walpole’s letter of 1779 on how people did before tea and sugar illustrates Mintz’s account of necessities.
Smith pairs the Complete Confectioner and Raffald as English eighteenth-century cookbooks that used sugar in almost every recipe.
Mazumdar: the rapid growth of Java’s sugar under the Dutch company is what gave Batavian sugar its hold on Surat.
Mazumdar: after the Dutch lost Taiwan in the 1660s and Chinese coasts were evacuated, they turned to Southeast Asian and Indian sources.
Walvin gauges the Americas’ exports by the proliferation of refineries in Antwerp and Amsterdam.
Walvin: by 1650 much of Barbados’s central forest had been destroyed by the new plantations.
Walvin: the islands’ value to Britain and France is why the revolt in Saint-Domingue was ‘much more than a colonial issue’.
